results.result: Premature eye opening in ferrets causes profound alterations in temporal frequency tuning, characterized by increased low-pass responses and broadened temporal frequency bandwidths. EO1contra and EO2 cells exhibited significantly elevated low-pass index values (0.35 and 0.33 vs. 0.20 in controls) and all early-opened groups showed significantly wider absolute temporal frequency bandwidths (4.7-5.1 octaves vs. 4.1 octaves in controls, p<0.002).
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C32-C46, and C111-C115 provide converging quantitative evidence from electrophysiological recordings with appropriate statistical analyses (Linear Mixed Effects Models). The data show consistent patterns across multiple measures (low-pass indices, bandwidths, L50/H50 cutoffs) with significant p-values. The findings are supported by visual representations in Figures 3A-I and supplementary figures.

results.result: Premature eye opening produces modest changes in orientation and direction selectivity. Orientation selectivity was slightly elevated in EO1contra (0.52, p<0.024) and EO2 neurons (0.54, p<0.016) compared to control (0.42), while direction selectivity was slightly reduced in EO1ipsi neurons (0.24, p<0.027) compared to control (0.29). The distributions of preferred orientations and directions did not differ significantly across groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C23-C31 are supported by electrophysiological data with appropriate statistical testing (LMEM and chi-square tests). The effects are small but statistically significant for some comparisons, and the authors appropriately characterize these as 'slight' changes. The lack of distributional differences (C30, C31) provides additional context that the changes are quantitative rather than qualitative.

results.result: Spatial frequency tuning was minimally affected by premature eye opening. No significant differences were observed in peak spatial frequency preferences across groups (control: 0.031 cpd; EO1ipsi: 0.045 cpd, p<0.19; EO1contra: 0.031 cpd, p<0.949; EO2: 0.042 cpd, p<0.362). Low-pass and high-pass indices showed only modest changes, and bandwidth measurements revealed no significant effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C47-C57 are supported by comprehensive electrophysiological measurements with appropriate statistical analyses. The lack of significant differences is well-documented across multiple spatial frequency parameters (peak preferences, low-pass/high-pass indices, bandwidths), providing strong evidence that spatial frequency tuning is relatively preserved despite premature visual experience.

results.result: Premature eye opening causes long-lasting bilateral increases in spontaneous firing rates. Spontaneous firing rates were markedly elevated in both EO1ipsi (11.1 Hz, p<1.09e-4), EO1contra (6.6 Hz, p<0.0132), and EO2 (6.6 Hz, p<0.0248) hemispheres compared to control (2.6 Hz). This bilateral effect suggests a global change in circuit excitability not restricted to cells viewing through the prematurely opened eye.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C6, C68-C73 are strongly supported by electrophysiological data showing significant increases in spontaneous activity across all experimental conditions, including the ipsilateral hemisphere. The bilateral nature of the effect (C5, C6) is particularly compelling evidence for a global circuit change. Statistical significance is robust (p<0.0248 or better), and the interpretation (C73) is reasonable given the persistence of effects measured at P55-68.

results.result: Peak visual responses were unchanged by premature eye opening (control: 7.0 Hz; EO1ipsi: 6.4 Hz, p<0.600; EO1contra: 10.1 Hz, p<0.518; EO2: 10.5 Hz, p<0.295), but response suppression below baseline was significantly elevated, particularly in EO1ipsi cells (7.0 Hz, p<1.59e-9) compared to control (2.1 Hz).
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C67 are supported by electrophysiological data with appropriate statistical analyses. The dissociation between unchanged peak responses and increased suppression is well-documented. The particularly strong effect in EO1ipsi cells (p<1.59e-9) is notable and statistically robust. Figure 5A-B provides visual confirmation of these findings.

results.result: The authors interpret the temporal frequency tuning deficits as suggestive of motion processing impairments and propose that premature visual experience in ferrets may model aspects of visual deficits observed in very premature human infants. They suggest that broadened temporal frequency tuning could impair discrimination of temporal frequency and speed of moving stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C74, C75, C8, and C103 represent interpretations and extrapolations from the experimental data. While the temporal frequency deficits are well-documented (Result 1), the connection to motion processing (C74, C75) is inferential and would require behavioral testing to confirm. The link to human prematurity (C103) is speculative, though the authors appropriately cite relevant literature (C100-C102). These interpretations are reasonable but not directly tested.

results.result: The authors speculate that closed eyelids in altricial mammals may serve to protect the developing visual system from high luminance, high contrast, and high spatial frequency stimulation until circuits are ready for visual experience refinement.
results.evaluation: Claims C9 and C105 are explicitly speculative (C9 states 'we speculate'). While the experimental data showing lasting deficits from premature vision are consistent with this hypothesis, the evolutionary interpretation is not directly tested. The speculation is reasonable given the findings but represents a hypothesis for future investigation rather than a demonstrated result.

results.result: The experimental design involved opening ferret eyes at P25 (during retinal wave period), providing 8 hours of visual experience over 4 days, and recording from monocular V1 at P55-68. The study used 27 female ferrets: 17 with one eye opened early, 4 with both eyes opened early, and 11 controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C20 and C106-C110 describe the experimental methodology and are well-documented in the Materials and Methods section. The timing is appropriately chosen based on cited developmental milestones (C16, C17 supported by citations). The sample sizes and recording locations are clearly stated. The methodology is sound for addressing the research questions.

results.result: The manuscript establishes the developmental context by citing prior work showing that mammalian visual system development proceeds in two stages: an early experience-independent stage guided by molecular cues and spontaneous activity, followed by an experience-dependent refinement stage. By P42 in ferrets, most visual response properties have reached adult-like levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C10, C11, C21, C22 are background claims supported by appropriate citations to established literature (Katz and Shatz 1996; Wong 1999; Li et al. 2006; Chapman and Stryker 1993; Issa et al. 1999). These provide the necessary developmental framework for interpreting the experimental findings. The citations appear appropriate and the characterization of prior work is accurate.

results.result: The authors contextualize their findings by comparing to prior altered-rearing studies, noting that dark-reared ferrets show poor direction selectivity but not strong temporal frequency deficits, strobe-reared cats show direction and motion sensitivity changes, and temporal frequency tuning is not rapidly modified by brief exposure after natural eye opening.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C83 are supported by appropriate citations to prior literature (Imbert and Buisseret 1975; Li et al. 2006; Kennedy and Orban 1983; Ritter et al. 2017; Bissen et al. 2025). The comparisons help establish the novelty of the temporal frequency deficits observed in this study. The characterization of prior work appears accurate based on the citations provided.

results.result: The authors establish clinical relevance by noting the rising population of very premature human infants who receive visual stimulation during the presensory period, and that such infants exhibit visual deficits including motion perception impairments and sometimes lowered visual acuity, even when brain damage and retinal problems are excluded.
results.evaluation: Claims C12, C13, C100-C102 are supported by appropriate citations to clinical literature (Crump et al. 2019; Colonnese et al. 2010; Ortibus et al. 2009; Atkinson and Braddick 2007; Jain et al. 2022). The characterization of the clinical population and their visual deficits provides important motivation for the study. The citations appear appropriate and the clinical context is accurately represented.

results.result: The authors discuss potential mechanisms by noting that visual input can drive activity through closed lids, GABAergic signaling switches occur by P21-23, inhibitory cells show activity patterns associated with orientation columns before eye opening but lack orientation selectivity, homeostatic mechanisms operate during critical periods, and retinal waves show interhemispheric coordination.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C96 are mechanistic background claims supported by appropriate citations to prior literature (Krug et al. 2001; Akerman et al. 2002; Mulholland et al. 2021; Chang and Fitzpatrick 2022; Desai et al. 1999; Hengen et al. 2013; Bock et al. 2012; Weliky and Katz 1999; Murcia-Belmonte et al. 2019). These provide context for interpreting the bilateral effects and potential circuit-level changes. The citations appear appropriate.

results.result: EO1ipsi cells exhibited slightly higher temporal frequency preferences (p<0.021) compared to other cell types.
results.evaluation: Claim C35 is supported by statistical analysis (LMEM, p<0.021) and shown in Figure 3E. This finding is somewhat unexpected given that EO1ipsi cells viewed through the naturally-opened eye, but the statistical support is clear. This may relate to the bilateral effects discussed in Result 4.

results.result: Prior studies in other species (bobwhite quail and rats) have shown that premature sensory experience causes behavioral and perceptual deficits, including loss of species-specific visual selectivity, altered auditory processing, and asymmetric locomotor reactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C99 are supported by appropriate citations to prior work (Lickliter 2018; Sleigh and Lickliter 1995; Foreman and Altaha 1991). These comparisons across species strengthen the generalizability of the finding that premature sensory experience has lasting consequences. The characterization of prior work appears accurate.

results.result: Ferrets are an appropriate model for studying premature visual experience because they undergo long postnatal development, are born with eyes closed for 30-35 days, and in the wild raise young in relatively dark nests.
results.evaluation: Claims C14, C15, C84 establish the rationale for using ferrets as a model system. C15 is supported by citation to Issa et al. 1999, and C84 by Ruggiero et al. 1994. The characterization of ferret development and natural history is accurate and provides important context for the experimental manipulation.

results.result: The authors conclude that premature patterned vision has a long-lasting impact on the development of receptive fields in visual cortex, regardless of clinical relevance to human vision.
results.evaluation: Claim C104 is a summary statement supported by the collective experimental findings (Results 1-5). The lasting nature of the effects is demonstrated by measurements at P55-68, well after the critical period closure. This is a well-supported conclusion from the experimental data.

results.result: Premature eye opening in ferrets resulted in altered temporal frequency tuning, with many cells exhibiting low-pass tuning, increased temporal frequency bandwidths, and stronger responses at low temporal frequencies. These changes were particularly pronounced in EO1contra and EO2 groups, with significant increases in absolute temporal frequency bandwidth across all early-opened groups.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirmed these findings, stating 'marked differences in temporal frequency tuning' and noting that 'temporal frequency bandwidth for responses evoked from early-opened contralateral eyes were broader than for controls.' The editor described this as 'convincing evidence' that 'eye opening at this time impacts temporal frequency tuning.'

results.result: Orientation and direction selectivity showed minimal changes following premature eye opening, with only slight elevations in orientation selectivity in EO1contra and EO2 neurons, and a slight reduction in direction selectivity in EO1ipsi neurons. Overall distributions of orientation and direction preferences did not differ significantly across groups.
results.evaluation: Reviewers confirmed these findings, stating 'little or no difference in mean orientation and direction selectivity' as a result of early eye opening. This was accepted without challenge as part of the overall pattern showing selective effects on temporal but not spatial or orientation properties.

results.result: Spatial frequency tuning was minimally affected by premature eye opening, with no significant differences in peak spatial frequency preferences across experimental groups and only modest changes in low-pass and high-pass indices.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly noted 'little or no difference in...spatial frequency tuning, as a result of early eye opening.' This finding was accepted as part of the overall conclusion that premature eye opening selectively affects temporal processing while leaving spatial frequency tuning largely intact.

results.result: Spontaneous firing rates were markedly elevated in both hemispheres following premature eye opening, with the largest increases in EO1ipsi hemispheres. This bilateral elevation suggests a global change in circuit excitability that persists long-term and is not restricted to neurons viewing through the prematurely opened eye.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirmed this finding, stating 'premature eye-opening increased spontaneous rates in all test configurations' and that the editor noted 'elevates spontaneous firing rates' as convincing evidence. The bilateral nature and interpretation of global circuit changes were accepted without challenge.

results.result: Peak visual responses did not differ significantly across groups, but response suppression below baseline was substantially elevated in animals with prematurely opened eyes, particularly in EO1ipsi cells. This indicates altered inhibitory mechanisms without changes in maximal excitatory drive.
results.evaluation: Reviewers noted 'changes in firing rate and sign of response to visual stimuli' and specifically mentioned that 'firing rates recorded from the ipsilateral cortex were strongly suppressed.' The dissociation between unchanged peak responses and increased suppression was accepted as part of the overall findings.

results.result: The authors interpret their findings as demonstrating that premature visual experience alters circuit excitability and visual receptive fields, particularly temporal processing, which may translate to deficits in motion processing and the ability to distinguish temporal frequency or speed of moving stimuli. They suggest this is consistent with motion processing deficits observed in premature human infants.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirmed this interpretation, noting the changes 'are especially interesting as they relate to deficits seen in prematurely delivered children' and that the findings 'will have great relevance for neuroscientists studying visual system development, particularly in the context of premature birth.' The connection to motion processing was accepted as a reasonable interpretation.

results.result: The authors speculate that closed eyelids in altricial mammals may serve to protect the visual system from premature patterned visual experience until circuits are properly established, preventing exposure to high luminance, contrast, and spatial frequency stimulation before the system is ready.
results.evaluation: While explicitly speculative, reviewers accepted this interpretation without challenge. One reviewer noted the experiments 'demonstrate clearly that premature patterned vision has a long-lasting impact on the development of receptive fields' and that results 'will be foundational for future studies.' The protective function hypothesis was treated as a reasonable conclusion from the data.

results.result: The experimental design involved opening ferret eyes at P25 (when retinal waves are still occurring and V1 is responsive through closed lids), providing 8 hours of visual exposure over 4 days, and recording from monocular V1 at P55-68 in 27 ferrets across control and experimental groups.
results.evaluation: Reviewers praised the experimental design and execution, noting 'the laboratory has long experience in quantitative studies' and 'the experiments are so difficult to perform and so carefully described.' The editor called it a 'carefully conducted study.' The methodology was accepted without substantive critique.

results.result: The manuscript establishes background context about visual system development proceeding in two stages (spontaneous activity-driven followed by experience-dependent), the relevance to premature human infants, and the ferret as an appropriate model system with eyes closed for 30-35 days and adult-like tuning properties by P42.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this background framing without challenge, noting the study 'aims to understand how the early visual experience of premature infants induces lasting deficits' and acknowledging the ferret as 'a well-established animal model for visual development.' The developmental framework was treated as established knowledge.

comparisons.comparison: Both OpenEval and peer reviewers strongly support the temporal frequency tuning findings (C2, C3, C32-C46, C111-C115). OpenEval emphasizes the quantitative evidence and statistical rigor, while peer reviewers describe 'marked differences' and 'convincing evidence.' Both evaluations are aligned in finding this evidence compelling. Note that C35 appears in both, though OpenEval separately highlights it in R13.

Perfect agreement on orientation and direction selectivity findings (C4, C23-C31). Both evaluations support that early eye opening produces little or no difference in these properties. OpenEval notes the effects are 'small but statistically significant' for some comparisons, while peer reviewers accept this as part of the selective effects pattern.

Complete alignment on spatial frequency tuning preservation (C7, C47-C57). Both evaluations support that spatial frequency tuning remains largely intact despite premature visual experience. OpenEval emphasizes the comprehensive nature of measurements across multiple parameters, while peer reviewers accept this as demonstrating selective effects on temporal but not spatial processing.

Strong agreement on spontaneous activity increases (C5, C6, C68-C73). Both evaluations support the bilateral effects and global circuit change interpretation. OpenEval highlights the statistical robustness (p<0.0248 or better) and persistence of effects, while peer reviewers affirm the finding across all test configurations without challenge.

Both evaluations support the dissociation between unchanged peak responses and increased suppression (C58-C67). OpenEval emphasizes the particularly strong effect in EO1ipsi cells (p<1.59e-9), while peer reviewers note the changes in firing rate and suppression patterns. Both accept the findings as well-documented.

Divergence in evaluation type: OpenEval rates C74, C75, C8, C103 as UNCERTAIN, noting these are interpretations requiring behavioral testing to confirm the motion processing connection. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, accepting the interpretation and noting relevance to premature birth deficits. OpenEval is more cautious about inferential claims, while peer reviewers accept them as reasonable interpretations. Note that C104 is included in peer R6 but OpenEval addresses it separately in R16.

Divergence in evaluation type: OpenEval rates the evolutionary speculation (C9, C105) as UNCERTAIN, explicitly noting it is speculative and represents a hypothesis rather than demonstrated result. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, accepting it as a reasonable conclusion. Both acknowledge the speculative nature, but differ on whether this warrants an UNCERTAIN vs SUPPORTED designation.

Perfect agreement on methodology (C16-C20, C106-C110). Both evaluations strongly support the experimental design and execution. OpenEval notes the methodology is 'sound for addressing the research questions,' while peer reviewers praise the 'carefully conducted study' and 'difficult to perform' experiments. Both accept without substantive critique.

Both evaluations support the background framework claims (C1, C10, C11, C21, C22), though peer R9 also includes C12-C15 which OpenEval addresses separately in R11 and R15. OpenEval emphasizes appropriate citations to established literature, while peer reviewers accept the developmental framework as established knowledge without challenge.

OpenEval separately highlights C35 (EO1ipsi temporal frequency effects) as noteworthy given cells viewed through naturally-opened eye, while peer reviewers include this claim within their broader evaluation of temporal frequency findings (R1) without special comment. Both support the finding but OpenEval gives it individual attention.

OpenEval addresses C104 (lasting effects summary) separately as SUPPORTED by collective experimental findings, while peer reviewers include it within their evaluation of clinical relevance and interpretation (R6). Both support the claim but group it differently in their evaluations.

OpenEval separately evaluates clinical literature background (C12, C13, C100-C102) as SUPPORTED with appropriate citations, while peer reviewers include C12-C13 within their broader background framework evaluation (R9). Both accept these claims but OpenEval provides more granular analysis of the clinical context.

OpenEval separately evaluates ferret model rationale (C14, C15, C84) as SUPPORTED, while peer reviewers include C14-C15 within their broader background evaluation (R9). Both accept the ferret model as appropriate but OpenEval provides dedicated analysis of the model system justification.

OpenEval evaluates comparative literature claims (C76-C83) as SUPPORTED, noting appropriate citations establishing novelty of temporal frequency deficits. No corresponding peer review evaluation found - peer reviewers did not separately address these comparative literature claims.

OpenEval evaluates mechanistic background claims (C85-C96) as SUPPORTED with appropriate citations for interpreting bilateral effects and circuit-level changes. No corresponding peer review evaluation found - peer reviewers did not separately address these mechanistic background claims.

OpenEval evaluates cross-species comparison claims (C97-C99) as SUPPORTED, noting citations strengthening generalizability of premature sensory experience findings. No corresponding peer review evaluation found - peer reviewers did not separately address these cross-species comparisons.
